text: Because all I had read were books. <break time="0.8s" /> In which characters were foreign. <break time="0.8s" /> I had become convinced. <break time="0.8s" /> That books, by their very nature, had to have foreigners in them. <break time="0.8s" /> And had to be about things. <break time="0.8s" /> With which I could not personally identify. <break time="0.8s" /> Now, things changed. <break time="0.8s" /> When I discovered African books. <break time="0.8s" /> There were not many of them available. <break time="0.8s" /> And they were not quite as easy to find. <break time="0.8s" /> As the foreign books. <break time="0.8s" /> But because of writers like Chinua Achebe and Camara Laye. <break time="0.8s" /> I went through a mental shift. <break time="0.8s" /> In my perception of literature. <break time="0.8s" /> I realized. <break time="0.8s" /> That people like me. <break time="0.8s" /> Girls with skin the color of chocolate. <break time="0.8s" /> Whose kinky hair could not form ponytails. <break time="0.8s" /> Could also exist. <break time="0.8s" /> In literature. <break time="0.8s" /> I started to write. <break time="0.8s" /> About things I recognized. <break time="0.8s" /> Now, I loved. <break time="0.8s" /> Those American and British books I read. <break time="0.8s" /> They stirred my imagination. <break time="0.8s" /> They opened up new worlds for me. <break time="0.8s" /> But the unintended consequence. <break time="0.8s" /> Was that I did not know. <break time="0.8s" /> That people like me could exist in literature. <break time="0.8s" /> So what the discovery of African writers did for me. <break time="0.8s" /> Was this. <break time="0.8s" /> It saved me. <break time="0.8s" /> From having a single story. <break time="0.8s" /> Of what books are. <break time="0.8s" /> I come from a conventional, middle class Nigerian family. <break time="0.8s" /> My father was a professor. <break time="0.8s" /> My mother was an administrator. <break time="0.8s" /> And so we had. <break time="0.8s" /> As was the norm. <break time="0.8s" /> Live in domestic help. <break time="0.8s" /> Who would often come from nearby rural villages. <break time="0.8s" /> So the year I turned eight. <break time="0.8s" /> We got a new house boy. <break time="0.8s" /> His name was Fide. <break time="0.8s" /> The only thing my mother told us about him. <break time="0.8s" /> Was that his family was very poor. <break time="0.8s" /> My mother sent. <break time="0.8s" /> Yams and rice, and our old clothes. <break time="0.8s" /> To his family. <break time="0.8s" /> And when I did not finish my dinner. <break time="0.8s" /> My mother would say. <break time="0.8s" /> Finish your food, Do you not know, People like Fides family have nothing. <break time="0.8s" /> So I felt enormous pity. <break time="0.8s" /> For Fides family.
